title: Last Car in the Garage
story: A small parking garage logs a ticket number at the gate twice for every car: once when it drives in and once when it drives out. The log is one long list of ticket numbers, in no useful order, because cars come and go all day.

At closing time exactly one car is still inside, so exactly one ticket number shows up only once. The attendant wants that number, and the gate computer is tiny: it can read the log once but has almost no spare memory.
task: Write carStillInside(log). Every ticket number in log appears exactly twice, except one that appears exactly once. Return that number.
Aim for one pass over the log and O(1) extra memory: no map, no set, no sorted copy.
constraints: Exactly one number appears once. Every other number appears exactly twice.

examples.explanation: 512 came in and went out. So did 87. 340 appears only once, so that car is still inside.
The two 4s sit next to each other, but the two 9s and the lone 2 do not. Do not assume partners are neighbours. The answer is 2.

hints: Forget memory limits for a moment. What is x XOR x for any number x? And what is x XOR 0?
XOR of a number with itself is 0, and XOR with 0 changes nothing. Also, XOR does not care about order: a ^ b ^ a equals a ^ a ^ b.
So what happens if you XOR every ticket in the log together? Each pair cancels to 0, wherever its two halves sit. What is left?
Start with result = 0 and XOR in every number of the log. The pairs cancel out, and result ends up holding the one ticket with no partner.
bruteForce: Count every ticket in a hash map and return the one with count 1. That is O(n) time, but it stores up to n / 2 numbers, which the gate computer cannot afford. Checking each ticket against every other one uses no memory but costs O(n²): with 30,001 entries that is about 900 million comparisons.
Sorting and then comparing neighbours in steps of two works with little memory, but it still costs O(n log n) and needs a sortable copy or permission to reorder the log.

js: * @param {number[]} log  every ticket twice except one

tests.note: the answer is 0 and sits at the start
the answer is at the very end
pairs are not next to each other
1 ^ 2 = 3: summing or OR-ing the distinct values would be wrong
the lone ticket is 0, in the middle: a "found yet?" check on the value 0 breaks

js: result ^= ticket; // pairs cancel: x ^ x = 0
py: result ^= ticket  # pairs cancel: x ^ x = 0
walkthrough: XOR compares two numbers bit by bit and gives 1 where the bits differ. Two facts do all the work here: x ^ x = 0, and x ^ 0 = x. Order does not matter, so every pair in the log cancels out no matter how far apart its halves are.
The middle values (13, 11) look like nonsense, and that is fine. Only the final value matters.
solution.takeaway: XOR is a cancel button: anything that appears an even number of times vanishes. Reach for it when values come in pairs and you need the odd one out, or when you must find a difference without extra memory.
